claims.text: Engineered chemically and structurally distinct interfaces govern resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings.
Multilayer interfaces act as effective barriers to dislocation motion.
Multilayer interfaces act as effective barriers to creep.
Dislocation pile-up at the interfaces produces local back-stresses.
Interface-induced back-stresses inhibit time-dependent plastic deformation.
Strain partitioning between contrasting layers delays slip and creep.
High-entropy phases possess inherently high lattice distortion that delays plastic flow.
High-entropy phases exhibit sluggish atomic diffusion that delays slip and creep.
The combination of interface blocking, strain partitioning, lattice distortion, and sluggish diffusion reduces creep rate relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
The proposed multilayers contain alternating layers that differ chemically and microstructurally.
The proposed interfaces are coherent or semi-coherent and separate layers with differing lattice parameters or compositions.
At otherwise identical overall composition and test conditions, multilayer coatings will have lower creep rates than homogeneous single-phase coatings.
At otherwise identical overall composition and test conditions, multilayer coatings will exhibit less steady-state deformation than homogeneous single-phase coatings.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate below approximately 0.5 times the melting temperature, where interface degradation is minimal.
The proposed mechanism applies when layer thicknesses are in the nanometer-to-sub-micrometer range.
At higher temperatures, diffusion-induced interface instability may dominate deformation.
Excessively thick layers may allow competing deformation mechanisms to dominate.
Processing-induced variation in interface quality and long-term interface stability may alter the measured creep response.
